ai.definition: Low-Cost Maternal Health Diagnostics refers to portable ultrasound and screening tools designed to detect pre-eclampsia and postpartum haemorrhage risks in resource-limited settings. These devices are intended for non-specialist operators, making them accessible and cost-effective.
ai.howItWorks: The technology utilizes handheld probes equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) guidance systems that assist non-specialist healthcare workers in performing ultrasounds and other diagnostic tests accurately. This AI helps in interpreting the results, ensuring reliable diagnoses even without extensive medical training.
ai.problemSolved: These diagnostics address the issue of maternal mortality by providing early detection of conditions like pre-eclampsia and postpartum haemorrhage, which are major contributors to maternal deaths, especially in resource-limited settings where access to specialized care is limited.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves producing handheld probes with integrated AI guidance systems. The process requires precision in component assembly and software integration to ensure reliability and accuracy.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the hardware for portability and ease of use, developing AI algorithms for diagnostic interpretation, and integrating these components into a user-friendly system. Quality control is crucial to ensure consistent performance across all units.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development of robust AI systems, the production costs of high-quality medical-grade probes, and the need for rigorous testing and validation before deployment in clinical settings.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to transition from lab research to early commercial stages as it gains more validation through pilot programs and real-world applications.
ai.regulation: Regulatory approval will be necessary, involving compliance with medical device standards and guidelines specific to maternal health diagnostics. This may include clinical trials to demonstrate safety and efficacy in diverse settings.
ai.risks: Risks include technical challenges in ensuring accurate diagnoses across different populations, regulatory hurdles, and the need for ongoing support and training of healthcare workers using these devices.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain given the initial high costs of development and deployment. However, as the technology gains traction and scales, it could become a cost-effective solution with potential for widespread adoption in low-resource settings.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include integrating additional diagnostic capabilities, improving AI accuracy through more extensive training data, and expanding the range of conditions that can be detected using these devices.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking processes required for medical-grade components.

glossary.def: A pregnancy complication characterized by high blood pressure and signs of damage to another organ system, usually the liver and kidneys.
Excessive bleeding that occurs after childbirth, which can be life-threatening if not promptly treated.
The use of artificial intelligence to assist in the interpretation and accuracy of medical diagnostic tests performed by non-specialist operators.

subsystems.name: Handheld ultrasound probe
subsystems.role: generates and receives ultrasound waves to image the fetus, placenta and uterus.
parts: piezoelectric transducer array (typically 2–5 MHz for obstetric depth)

subsystems.name: AI guidance software
subsystems.role: helps a non-specialist acquire usable images and interpret them.

subsystems.name: Pre-eclampsia screening kit
subsystems.role: detects the warning signs of high blood pressure and protein in urine.
parts: urine protein test strips or reader

subsystems.name: Postpartum haemorrhage risk tools
subsystems.role: estimates blood loss and identifies women who need escalation.
parts: quantitative blood-loss measurement (e.g. calibrated drapes or weighing)
shock index calculation from pulse and blood pressure

subsystems.name: Mobile app and data layer
subsystems.role: runs the algorithms, stores results and supports referral.

subsystems.name: Training and support system
subsystems.role: teaches operators and maintains image and decision quality.

buildSteps.title: Design the transducer
buildSteps.detail: Choose frequency, element count and aperture to image at depths of 5–20 cm, then simulate acoustic performance to balance resolution and penetration.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the probe
buildSteps.detail: Dice a piezoelectric ceramic, bond it to backing and matching layers, and connect it to custom integrated circuits that digitise the echoes.

buildSteps.title: Develop the AI models
buildSteps.detail: Collect and annotate ultrasound images and clinical data from diverse populations; train algorithms for plane recognition, measurement and abnormality flags; validate against expert review.

buildSteps.title: Build the app
buildSteps.detail: Integrate probe drivers, on-device or cloud inference, and a simple interface usable by midwives and nurses with limited ultrasound training.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the screening kit
buildSteps.detail: Pair the probe with a validated blood-pressure monitor and urine tests, calibrate all components, and package them in a rugged, cleanable case.

buildSteps.title: Run clinical studies
buildSteps.detail: Compare the package against standard care in the target settings; measure whether it improves detection of pre-eclampsia and postpartum haemorrhage risk.

buildSteps.title: Obtain regulatory approval
buildSteps.detail: Submit evidence of safety and effectiveness to national regulators and pursue WHO prequalification so the kit can be procured widely.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture at scale
buildSteps.detail: Set up production lines with quality control, ensure spare parts and battery replacement, and keep unit cost low enough for public health budgets.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and train
buildSteps.detail: Distribute to clinics, train midwives and nurses, and establish remote support and maintenance so the tools stay working.

prerequisites.why: smartphone-era chips have made handheld probes possible at low cost.
some tools can estimate gestational age or fetal presentation, but comprehensive risk screening is not yet standard.
they provide the screen, processor and connectivity for the app.
frameworks are emerging but slow, and approvals must cover both hardware and software.
many target clinics have intermittent power and network, so the kit must work offline and on battery.
shortages of skilled sonographers are the gap the tool aims to fill, but some training is always needed.

pathway.milestone: handheld ultrasound probes are commercially available and used in high-resource settings; pilots in low-resource settings show feasibility.
pathway.unlocks: portable imaging where no sonographer is available.

pathway.milestone: AI-guided tools for non-specialists are validated in trials for specific tasks such as gestational age and fetal lie.
pathway.unlocks: safe task-shifting to midwives and nurses.

pathway.milestone: integrated packages for pre-eclampsia and postpartum haemorrhage risk are deployed at scale with training and supply chains.
pathway.unlocks: earlier detection and referral, reducing deaths from the leading causes of maternal mortality.

pathway.milestone: continuous maternal monitoring and predictive analytics linked to referral networks.
pathway.unlocks: a shift from crisis response to proactive care in the settings where deaths are concentrated.
